title: Advancement Ledger for Parents Funding Jobless Kids
one_liner: A living ledger plus a state-specific estate addendum that records what Boomer parents advance to struggling adult children, so the inheritance later comes out fair and siblings do not end up in court.
customer: Parents aged 65-80 with $500K-$5M estates and two or more adult children, at least one of whom is unemployed or underemployed. Channel: estate attorneys, elder-law firms and RIAs, who white-label it. Payers: parents ($199 setup plus $12-20/mo), firms ($500/mo white label) or RIAs (per-household fee).
problem: The AI hiring freeze (NY Fed: recent-grad underemployment about 42%) turns Mom and Dad into the bank of last resort. Rent, tuition, car and 'bridge loans' flow unevenly to siblings, undocumented and undecided as gift, loan or advancement against inheritance. Decades later, executors and trustees face contested history and estate litigation, and families break. Wealth advisors say family meetings are essential, yet nobody tracks advances.
solution: Parents log each advance in a simple app and tag it as gift, loan or advancement. The child e-acknowledges it. Optional interest at the AFR turns it into a formal promissory note. The system flags amounts near gift-tax-return thresholds (annual exclusion about $19K). It produces a running equalization statement the attorney can attach to a will or trust with a state-specific 'hotchpot' clause. An annual sibling-transparent 'family statement' replaces secrecy. Repayment or forgiveness schedules kick in when a child gets re-employed.
why_now: Millions of 22-35-year-olds face a low-hire market while Gen X and Millennial heirs are about to receive trillions (Cerulli: Gen X about $14T in the next decade). Federal student-loan caps reportedly tightened from July 2026 (verify), pushing more tuition onto family money. With a higher federal estate exemption (reportedly about $15M per person from 2026, verify), fewer estates are tax-driven and more are conflict-driven, so fairness documentation is now the main planning value.
revenue_model: $199 'Fair Share Package' (memo, ledger, 45-minute attorney review). $12-20/mo subscription. Attorney and RIA white label at $500/mo per firm or a per-household fee. Later: paid mediation add-on when siblings disagree.
non_obvious_insight: The AI jobs shock will show up in probate court a decade before it shows up in most statistics. Unequal parental support is the seed of the next generation of estate fights, and equalization is a data problem (a ledger), not a legal one. Parents will pay real money to keep their kids from fighting after they die.
first_30_days: With two friendly estate attorneys, draft an advancement memo and equalization clause for two states. Put up a landing page aimed at parents searching 'paying rent for my 26-year-old' and post in personal-finance and parenting communities. Sell the $199 package with a manual spreadsheet ledger to the first 25 families, then build the app around what they actually log. Ask 10 elder-law attorneys to co-present at seminars.

title: CMMC Enclave for CNC Shops
one_liner: A prebuilt, shop-floor-aware CUI enclave and evidence pack that gets 20-person machine shops through CMMC Level 2 without rebuilding their IT.
customer: Job shops and small manufacturers making parts for defense primes (castings, forgings, machined parts), roughly 30,000-plus firms in the defense supply base.
problem: CMMC Level 2 assessments for contract awards ramp up from Nov 2026 (verify dates). Shops keep CUI drawings on machine-side PCs and USB sticks, and generic CMMC consultants scope the entire company. Sub-tier suppliers lack IT staff and capital, exactly the bottleneck AIA-Bain describes.
solution: A managed enclave that isolates only the CAD/CAM and CNC controllers handling CUI, ships as a pre-configured appliance plus cloud tenant, and comes with policies, evidence collection and assessor liaison. Fixed monthly price, no consultants hourly.
why_now: Phase-in of the CMMC rule puts assessment on contracts through 2026-27, and primes are pushing flow-down requirements. Sub-tier financing is scarce, so shops need a low-capex option.
revenue_model: $800-2,500 per month per shop plus $5-15K onboarding. Channel through primes who will subsidize their suppliers' compliance.
non_obvious_insight: Scope reduction is the whole business. The winning product understands machine tool OT and draws a tight boundary around it, while horizontal CMMC vendors sell a heavy enterprise program.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 shops through a regional manufacturing extension partnership. Assemble the appliance from commodity parts. Sign one prime's supplier program as channel.

title: Recycled-Content Claim Defense Files
one_liner: Litigation-grade, SKU-level substantiation files for recycled-content claims, built on purchase-to-claim reconciliation rather than more certificates.
customer: General counsel and heads of sustainability at mid-market consumer brands ($100M-$2B revenue) with 'recycled' claims on pack, and retailer private-label teams.
problem: California vetoed AB 2253 (recycled-content claim substantiation) citing 'economic headwinds.' State PCR mandates are slipping (NJ to 2029). Mass-balance accounting is contested and no standard exists. Brands keep making claims for retailers and consumers, while the burden of proving them lands on legal departments via plaintiffs, AGs and retailer audits.
solution: A SKU-level claim file: verify supplier certificates, reconcile volume of certified resin bought against recycled-content claims across all SKUs, and produce a plain-language legal memo on which claims are safe. Add an annual refresh with change alerts. Partner with an insurer for defense-cost coverage credits.
why_now: The veto removed the one route to a state safe harbor and the mandate delays weaken the compliance pretext, so brands are exposed to claim risk without clear rules. Two years of contested mass-balance debate leave no accepted method.
revenue_model: $3-8K per SKU family for the initial file, $20-60K per year retainer, and referral fees from insurers and law firms.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody is short of certificates. Brands are short of reconciliation: a certificate proves a supplier's volume, not that a brand's claims across 400 SKUs are arithmetically supportable.
first_30_days: Build a spreadsheet reconciliation template. Partner with one litigation-defense law firm. Scrape retail listings for '% recycled' claims to find targets. Sell 5 paid claim audits at about $5K each.

title: Hallmark-Style Microdramas for Women 45+
one_liner: A genre studio making 60-episode vertical dramas (cozy mystery, faith-and-family, second-act romance) for the older female audience the romance-and-revenge apps under-serve, sold through web checkout.
customer: Women aged 40-65 in the US, UK, Canada and Australia paying via coin packs or weekly subscriptions. Aggregator apps such as ReelShort and DramaBox are a second customer as licensees.
problem: Microdramas are a roughly $11B global market, with about $1.3B a year of US spend, mostly women 30-60. Supply skews toward billionaire-romance, werewolf and revenge tropes. Genres this audience already pays for on Hallmark, Lifetime and faith networks are thin.
solution: Shoot 60-70 episode series for $50-90k on 8-day schedules with real actors, and use AI only in post (subtitles, cleanup, ADR), not for performers. Test three genres with $3k of Meta ads per pilot, license winners to aggregators for minimum guarantees, then push loyal viewers to your own web-checkout app.
why_now: Epic's April 2025 ruling stopped Apple charging fees on purchases made outside its store in the US, so a vertical-drama app can keep most of the margin on web checkout. Series cycle times are under two weeks, and the market has proven willingness to pay.
revenue_model: Coin and subscription revenue via own app (LTV-driven), plus aggregator licensing fees and minimum guarantees, plus brand integrations.
non_obvious_insight: The leaders optimized for early-adopter tropes. Viewers 45+ already pay for TV subscriptions, have cards on file, are cheap to reach on Facebook, and churn less. Scarcity of content for them is a supply gap, not a demand gap.
first_30_days: Shoot a 10-episode pilot for about $12k. Run a $3k ad test on three genres and pick the winner by cost per paying viewer. Pitch two aggregators for a minimum guarantee, and stand up a web paywall using an off-the-shelf subscription funnel tool.

title: Orphan Fleet Depot for Bankrupt-Maker Electric Buses
one_liner: Sustainment-as-a-service for school districts and transit agencies stuck with electric buses whose manufacturer went bankrupt, using the military's orphan-platform playbook (salvaged parts pool, configuration control, depot repair, availability guarantees).
customer: School districts, regional education service agencies and small transit agencies that own buses from failed OEMs (Lion Electric US buses, Proterra, and similar EV truck and bus makers), plus state grant administrators and cooperative-purchasing bodies that want the taxpayer-funded fleets running.
problem: When Lion Electric went through bankruptcy and its new owner voided prior U.S. warranties, districts were left with buses nobody would service. Some sourced parts themselves, some sidelined buses, and some went back to diesel. Proterra's transit business went through a similar handoff. Grant-funded buses that sit idle are a political and audit embarrassment. Dealers cannot fix proprietary battery, inverter and charge-port faults, and there is no parts channel.
solution: Run it like a military orphan-platform sustainment program. (1) Buy the bankruptcy estate's remaining parts, tooling and diagnostics at liquidation. (2) Build a per-VIN configuration database and a reverse-engineered diagnostic library. (3) Stand up a regional depot and a mobile repair van for line-replaceable units: contactors, DC-DC converters, charge ports, battery management modules and pack modules. (4) Buy sidelined orphan buses cheaply as cannibalization donors. (5) Sell a fixed annual sustainment contract per bus that guarantees a morning-route availability rate, backed by a shared spares pool across districts sized with readiness-based sparing math.
why_now: Lion's sale voided U.S. warranties (reported late 2025), so the 2025-26 school year is when the pain became real. The installed base of grant-funded EV buses is large and aging out of warranty, and subsidy rollbacks (the federal commercial clean vehicle credit ended for vehicles acquired after Sept 30, 2025) make further OEM failures likely. The parts estates of failed makers are cheapest to buy right now, before anyone else sees their value.
revenue_model: Annual sustainment contract of roughly $4-8k per bus with an availability guarantee, plus time-and-materials for depot repairs, spares-pool membership fees for districts that want priority access, and salvage and refurbished battery pack sales. Sold through cooperative purchasing vehicles so districts do not each run a bid.
non_obvious_insight: Orphaned does not mean unfixable. In most orphaned fleets, 5-10 recurring line-replaceable units cause most of the downtime. A small shared spares pool plus a configuration-controlled baseline can lift availability from a coin flip to about 90%. The right buyer is not one district's bus garage but a state agency or regional service center pooling many districts, because the sparing math only works at fleet-of-fleets scale. Military sustainers call this the DMSMS problem and solved it by owning the baseline instead of waiting for the OEM.
first_30_days: Build a list of about 20 districts that took Lion or similar deliveries in 2022-24 from press coverage and grant award lists. Offer one district a free 'orphan health check' on a stranded bus using generic diagnostic tools and an EV-experienced transit mechanic. Register as a bidder in the relevant bankruptcy and liquidation processes and ask for the parts inventory lists. Hire 1-2 retired transit or heavy-duty EV technicians. Sign three districts to a per-bus quarterly pilot and use their fault logs to identify the top recurring failure modes.

title: Calibration Target Network for Earth-Observation Startups
one_liner: Networked ground calibration targets that issue overpass-synchronized calibration certificates for EO satellites.
customer: EO and SAR constellation operators, analytics firms selling certified measurements (insurance, methane, deforestation), and government agencies.
problem: Every new imaging satellite needs geometric and radiometric calibration, mostly done ad hoc. As EO output becomes regulated evidence, buyers ask who certified the sensor, and no third party provides traceable, on-demand ground truth.
solution: Deploy SAR corner reflectors, spectral tarps and instrumented sites (GPS, weather, irradiance) at a handful of stable locations. Automatically log each satellite overpass and issue a calibration certificate. Offer custom validation sites and controlled-release campaigns for customers.
why_now: The EO sector is mature and government-anchored (Planet's large contracts and Pelican production doubling per the briefing). Regulated uses raise demand for traceability. Many new SAR and hyperspectral entrants launch each year.
revenue_model: $30-150k per year per constellation. Project fees for custom validation sites. Certificates sold to analytics customers.
non_obvious_insight: As EO becomes evidence, the bottleneck is ground presence synchronized with overpasses, not more data.
first_30_days: Pick two well-known desert sites and place a first set of low-cost reflectors and tarps. Offer free certificates to three SAR and optical startups in return for testimonials, and ask for paid annual plans after the first quarter.

title: Contingency Appeals for Denied Pet Insurance Claims
one_liner: Insurers rely on paperwork friction to keep denials uncontested; LLMs that assemble records and policy language make appeals cheap enough to work for a success fee.
customer: Pet owners with denied or reduced claims of roughly $1,500-$15,000 (pre-existing, bilateral, hereditary or 'curable' exclusion disputes), reached through owner communities and vet front desks.
problem: Premiums rose about 19.7% in 2025 while insured animals grew 9%, so owners are angry and paying more for coverage that may not pay. An appeal requires pulling every prior clinic's records, reading policy definitions and getting a vet statement. Most owners give up.
solution: Owner uploads the denial letter and policy. We automate records requests to past clinics, read records against the policy's definitions and the state's pet-insurance rules, draft the appeal with a contracted DVM's signed medical statement, file it, and escalate to the state insurance department if needed. Fee is 15-25% of recovered dollars, nothing upfront.
why_now: As of early 2026, 28 states had adopted or introduced versions of the NAIC Pet Insurance Model Act, which creates disclosure and pre-existing-condition hooks and formal complaint routes. LLMs can now read messy multi-clinic records cheaply. Premium hikes are driving search intent and anger.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 15-25% of recovered claims. Second product: anonymized denial-pattern intelligence sold to regulators, clinics and insurers who want fewer disputes.
non_obvious_insight: Denial rates are sustained by the cost of contesting, not by the merits. That cost was human labor. Once evidence assembly is near-free, the spread between 'denied' and 'overturned when documented' becomes a business, and it produces the best dataset on how insurers actually deny.
first_30_days: Post 'no win, no fee appeals' in pet-owner communities and take 30 cases. Contract one vet to sign statements at $75-150 each. Track overturn rate; kill criterion is under 20%. Check state public-adjuster and unauthorized-practice rules before charging a contingency fee.

title: Recipient-Priced Inboxes for Outbound Agents
one_liner: A gateway that lets busy people set a price to reach them and makes outbound AI agents bid for attention, refunding the bond when the message proves relevant.
customer: Outbound agents (fundraising, PR, recruiting sourcing, partnership and research-interview agents) that decide per message whether a reply is worth $1-$50 and pay a refundable bond. The recipient side is VC partners, journalists, podcast bookers, specialist physicians and procurement heads.
problem: Agents remove the cost of sending, so high-value inboxes are drowning. Generic AI outreach now gets under 1% replies in most B2B segments, and reaching one buyer takes 7+ touches. Filters are an arms race, and recipients earn nothing for their attention.
solution: The recipient sets a price ladder (for example $5 for a read-guarantee, $25 for a reply window) and rules. Unknown senders get an auto-reply, or an HTTP 402 for agents, carrying a payment link. The sender agent estimates expected value from its own conversion data and posts a refundable bond over MPP, x402 or card. With one tap the recipient marks the message relevant, which returns the bond, or irrelevant, which pays the recipient. We take 15-20% of forfeited bonds. Sender reputation lowers prices for good senders and prices out spammers.
why_now: Agentic outbound exploded in 2026, with agents choosing targets and follow-ups on their own and degrading deliverability. Programmatic micropayment rails now make a $2 bond collectible without a human. Recipients are actively looking for ways to filter AI outreach.
revenue_model: 15-20% of forfeited bonds plus a 5% fee on settled reads. Team-inbox and executive-assistant tiers for recipients, and an API plan for senders that want reputation scores.
non_obvious_insight: Pay-to-email has failed for 25 years because humans underprice their own outreach and hate friction. Agents compute expected value per message, so a price signal finally clears the market, and it only works when both sides are software. Letting the recipient earn money flips their incentive from blocking to hosting.
first_30_days: Build a Gmail and Chrome extension with an auto-reply rule and recruit 50 investors, journalists and podcast bookers through founder networks. Recruit 10 outbound-agent tools (fundraising, PR, recruiting) as senders. Settle bonds manually via Stripe at first and measure reply-quality uplift against free outreach. Charge the take rate from month 2.

title: Court-Rules MCP Server With a Deadline Warranty
one_liner: Effective-dated, human-verified court rules, judge standing orders and deadline math for one state at a time, exposed to any AI agent, with fee credits if a computed deadline is wrong.
customer: Solo and small firms (5 or fewer attorneys) in personal injury, family, criminal defense and landlord-tenant who already run Clio or MyCase and are starting to use Claude or ChatGPT agents. Later, legal-AI vendors that buy the rule set by API.
problem: Missed deadlines are among the most common malpractice claims (background knowledge, verify). General models know case law roughly but not this county's local rules, this judge's standing order (including AI-use certifications), or this year's fee schedule. The rules live as PDFs across thousands of court sites and change constantly, and big-firm docketing systems are priced and built for large firms.
solution: Start with one state pack, for example Texas civil. It holds statutes of limitation, civil procedure, local rules of the top counties and judge standing orders, each effective-dated with a hashed source PDF. MCP tools such as compute_deadline(event, court, date) and check_filing(court, judge, doc_type) return the date, the rule cites and a confidence flag. A deterministic engine does the date math (no LLM arithmetic), paid legal editors verify the high-use rules, and change alerts go out. A small warranty (fee credit plus capped reimbursement) backs the deadline output.
why_now: 8am's MyCase says 60+ firms, mostly 5 or fewer attorneys, adopted its Claude MCP connector (73 actions) in the first month, so small firms are now consuming practice tools through agents. Case law is open and the model is free, but local procedure is not in any frontier legal product.
revenue_model: $79-149/month per firm per state pack, an API license of $2-10k/month for legal-AI vendors, and a premium warranty tier.
non_obvious_insight: When the model is free and the corpus is open, the scarce asset is authoritative, effective-dated local procedure with a liability wrapper. Nobody can warrant an LLM's legal reasoning, but a rules engine plus editorial verification is exactly where a warranty is underwritable.
first_30_days: Pick one state and one practice area. Hand-build the 300 highest-frequency rules with two contract paralegals (about $8-10k), ship a free MCP server, and recruit 15 firms through a state solo and small-firm bar list. Charge $99/month after the trial, publish an accuracy audit, and keep the warranty to a $500 credit until loss data exists.

title: CAM and Insurance Pass-Through Audits for Micro-Tenants
one_liner: Read a small tenant's lease, recompute the landlord's annual reconciliation, and dispute overcharges inside the audit window, on contingency.
customer: Restaurants, salons, clinics, gyms and boutiques on NNN or modified-gross leases in strip centers and small retail, typically 1,000-5,000 sq ft.
problem: Landlord reconciliations of common-area, tax and insurance charges are opaque, and pass-throughs rose with property insurance and tax bills (prior knowledge). Audit rights exist in the lease but expire in weeks or months, and owners never read the lease. Rising costs are the top financial challenge for small firms.
solution: Upload the lease and reconciliation. An LLM extracts audit rights, caps, exclusions, gross-up, base year, admin fees and pro-rata share, recomputes the statement, drafts the audit request or dispute letter, calendars deadlines, and escalates to an auditor partner for contested items. Add a renewal-negotiation packet.
why_now: Long-context models read leases cheaply. Enterprise tenants have lease-audit firms, but micro-tenants were never worth the hourly rate.
revenue_model: 25-30% of amounts recovered, with a $99 flat triage fee for leases that show no error.
non_obvious_insight: The lever is the deadline, not the arithmetic. Most owners have never seen their own audit clause, and landlords count on that.
first_30_days: Collect 10 leases and reconciliations through a restaurant association or business improvement district. Run manual audits, measure the hit rate, sign the first contingency deals and refine the extraction.

title: PFAS Turf Audits and Replacement Planning
one_liner: Field-by-field PFAS and regulatory risk audits plus replacement bid packages for school districts and parks departments with aging synthetic turf.
customer: School district facilities directors, athletic directors, municipal parks and recreation departments and colleges.
problem: Thousands of synthetic fields installed in the 2010s are reaching end of life just as PFAS rules bite: New York's ban on selling PFAS-containing turf takes effect December 31, 2026, California's restriction on PFAS in covered surfaces began January 1, 2026, and other states (New Jersey, Maine) have bills to pause purchases. Districts do not know what is under their fields, may not be able to buy what they always bought, and face bond votes and parent pressure.
solution: A $2.5-8k audit per district: field inventory (age, product, manufacturer), lab testing of fibers and infill through an accredited partner, legal exposure summary, lifecycle-cost comparison of synthetic, PFAS-free, hybrid and natural grass, and turnkey bid documents; then project-management and referral fees.
why_now: 2026 effective dates, active parent and environmental groups, and pending state bills create urgent, budgeted decisions.
revenue_model: $2.5-8k audits, testing pass-through margin, 2-4 percent project-management fees on $500k-1.5M projects, supplier referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody owns 'what is my turf made of' data and manufacturers will not volunteer it. Sitting between district, lab and contractor makes you the neutral spec writer who controls the RFP.
first_30_days: Build a public-records inventory of turf fields in New York from bond documents and board minutes, pitch 50 districts, line up an accredited lab, and sell three audits.

title: Rotor Rescue: Scrapyard Magnet Pick-and-Pay
one_liner: A price-sheet-plus-gauss-meter program that pays scrapyards for magnet-dense motors and rotors they currently sell as steel and copper.
customer: Rare-earth magnet recyclers and magnet makers needing domestic recycled feed (they pay per kg with assay). Scrapyards, motor rebuilders and appliance/HVAC recyclers are the sellers.
problem: The rare-earth bottleneck is 'collection and disassembly rather than recovery chemistry.' Hard-drive magnet removal often costs more than the material is worth. Yards sell EV drive units, servo and elevator motors, and e-bike hub motors by copper and steel weight, and the NdFeB rotors go into the steel shred.
solution: Skip HDDs and target a short list of heavy, magnet-dense items. Yards get a phone app plus a $150 gauss meter that identifies magnet-bearing units and shows a payout per unit or per rotor. A mobile pull cell or the yard's own labor removes rotors. We aggregate and assay them, then sell a certified, traceable magnet-feed stream to recyclers.
why_now: The IEA puts China at about 90% of material recovery capacity. The DoD-MP deal and the Texas magnet campus create domestic pull, and DOE announced $134M for critical-mineral demonstrations in June 2026. Recyclers such as Cyclic Materials and IonicRE are funded and need feed.
revenue_model: Spread between the recycler's price per kg of assayed magnet feed and the yard payout plus pull cost. Optional premium for defense-traceable lots. Small SaaS fee for the identification and price app.
non_obvious_insight: Rare-earth economics fail on tiny magnets (HDDs) but work on a few heavy items. No one publishes a price by motor model, so yards do not know a rotor holds hundreds of grams to kilograms of NdFeB. Price discovery is the missing product, not a new chemistry.
first_30_days: Buy 5 gauss meters. Visit 10 auto shredders and motor shops and measure and photograph 200 units. Build a price sheet by model. Get an offtake LOI from one magnet recycler that needs feed. Pay 3 yards on the first 50 units and publish the results to recruit more.

title: WhatsApp Voice-Note Superintendent for Spec Builders
one_liner: A bilingual coordinator-plus-AI service that runs daily crew confirmations, headcounts and re-sequencing for a builder's two dozen subs over WhatsApp voice notes, priced per house.
customer: Small private and spec builders (20-300 homes a year) in Texas, Florida and the Southeast, and remodelers who juggle many subs.
problem: A typical home needs about two dozen subs. Foundations sit 30+ days waiting for crews, and one executive described 15-20 houses stuck 6+ weeks. Builders learn a crew is not coming days too late. Project software requires English typing and logins, and workers are wary of anything that looks like tracking. Procore's 20 agents serve larger GCs.
solution: Foremen keep sending Spanish voice notes on WhatsApp. The system transcribes them, extracts headcount, phase status and photos, and updates the schedule. A nearshore bilingual coordinator confirms tomorrow's crews by 5 p.m., calls backup crews when there is a gap, and sends the builder one exception report each morning. Privacy by design: counts and progress only, no IDs or location.
why_now: ICE arrests rose from 32,545 in May to 49,571 in July 2026. Crews can shrink overnight (a Minnesota roofing crew went from 80 to 6). Multilingual speech models and the WhatsApp Business API are mature, and PM incumbents are focused on big GCs.
revenue_model: $300-500 per active house per month, or $3-6K per month per builder. One coordinator handles 25-40 houses, so gross margin is high.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not scheduling math, it is that the people who know whether tomorrow's crew is coming do not use the software. The interface must be the phone and language they already use. The daily headcount is the leading indicator, and knowing a day earlier lets a builder re-sequence trades instead of idling a foundation.
first_30_days: Sign 3 builders with 10-20 active houses each through a home builders association. Hire one bilingual coordinator. Run it manually with WhatsApp and a shared sheet, add speech-to-text in week 2, and document five saved crew-days.

title: Crawlspace Robots for the 44-Year-Old House
one_liner: Small tracked robots that scan, photograph and eventually air-seal and insulate the crawlspaces and attics humans dread, starting as a quote-enabling survey service.
customer: Home inspectors, insurers and home-warranty firms (moisture and water-damage claims), and HVAC, insulation and foundation-repair contractors who need access before quoting. Later: weatherization programs.
problem: Median home age is 44 years, 62% of homeowners now choose repair over replace, and 78% of those with unstarted projects have no quotes. Contractors avoid the crawlspace visit because it is slow, dirty and unsafe, so inspectors skip it and quotes are guesses. It is the most avoided labor in the house.
solution: Phase 1: a low-cost tracked robot with camera, thermal and LiDAR plus a vision-language pipeline producing a 10-minute survey covering moisture, insulation, duct leaks, pest and mold signs and structural issues, sold as an add-on to inspectors and a pre-quote survey to contractors. Phase 2: tool attachments for air sealing and topping insulation. Phase 3: crawlspace-as-a-service retrofit fleet.
why_now: Cheap edge compute, reliable vision-language defect classification and low-cost thermal sensors. Labor shortages make anyone willing to crawl scarce. Insurers want moisture data and aging stock keeps growing.
revenue_model: $149-249 per survey (inspector add-on or contractor pre-quote), insurer report fees, later per-job retrofit revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The robot does not need to replace skilled trades, only the worst 20 minutes of their job. Access is the friction, and a proprietary library of real crawlspace conditions is the moat.
first_30_days: Build v0 from a hobby tracked chassis, action camera and thermal sensor (about $3K). Run 30 free surveys for 5 home inspectors and 2 insulation contractors. Track how often findings convert to jobs and test pricing.

title: Drive-By Lawsuit Shield for Marketing Stacks
one_liner: Scan and fix the text, website and review flows that trigger serial-plaintiff demand letters, and back it with a response pack.
customer: Local-service SMBs and small multi-location brands, sold mostly through local marketing agencies and agency resellers on GoHighLevel, Wix and Squarespace.
problem: Serial-plaintiff waves target small firms: text-message consent and quiet-hours claims, website accessibility claims, wiretap claims over chat widgets and tracking pixels, and the FTC's fake-and-gated-review rule (prior knowledge on the rules). Demands of $5-25k get settled blind. AI-generated marketing raises exposure: 83% of AI-using small firms use AI for writing or marketing.
solution: A scanner checks known triggers: SMS consent capture and state quiet hours, trackers and chat widgets without consent banners, basic accessibility failures, review-gating flows and unsubstantiated claims. It applies or guides fixes, keeps a provenance-stamped consent ledger, and provides a demand-letter response pack via a partner law firm. Defense-cost coverage can be added through an MGA.
why_now: SMBs are now running automated texting, AI-written content and review requests, and small businesses lack legal capacity to evaluate demands.
revenue_model: $19-49 per site or number per month, $499 per response pack, plus a share of insurance premiums.
non_obvious_insight: The vendor who sells the marketing tool never gets sued, but the owner does, and the agency is liable to its client. The buyer of protection is the agency reseller, not the owner.
first_30_days: Build scanners for three triggers and run free scans on 500 local sites. Sell reports to 10 agencies and sign a law-firm partner for the response pack.

title: Settlement Claim Autopilot for Ticket Buyers
one_liner: A privacy-first app that reconstructs a fan's ticket purchase history and files claims in ticketing settlements and refund orders, paid per validated claim by administrators and plaintiff firms.
customer: Settlement administrators and plaintiff firms, who pay per validated claim because they are judged on claim rates. Consumers use it free or pay a success fee.
problem: The FTC alleges $3.7B in resale fees from 2019-2024. Live Nation was found liable on monopolization in April 2026. In June 2026 the UK CMA ordered StubHub to refund 50,000+ customers, and World Cup ticket failures triggered class actions in New York and British Columbia. Claim rates in consumer settlements are typically low because buyers cannot reconstruct old purchases.
solution: Fans forward receipt emails or upload data exports (avoiding restricted Gmail scopes at launch). Local parsing rebuilds each purchase (event, price, fee, date) and matches it to open claim windows and prefilled forms. Sell it to administrators as a claims-acquisition channel, and keep watching for new live-events settlements.
why_now: A wave of ticketing liabilities is landing at once, and cheap models can parse messy receipts. Individual recoveries of about $30 are uneconomical for lawyers but work in batch.
revenue_model: $3-15 per validated claim from administrators and law firms, optional 10-15% consumer success fee, and later expansion to other settlement categories.
non_obvious_insight: The real buyer is the administrator or counsel measured on claim rate, not the consumer. Email receipts are better proof than memory, and automation turns tiny per-person recoveries into a scalable business.
first_30_days: Launch a landing page around the CMA StubHub refund order. Pitch 5 administrators and pilot one active claim. Test the receipt-forward parser with 500 users and negotiate a per-claim bounty.

title: Documentation-Review Copilot for Notified Bodies and Labs
one_liner: Software that triages and pre-checks manufacturers' technical files for the third-party assessors that CRA, Machinery, radio-cyber and AI Act rules are about to swamp.
customer: EU notified bodies, cybersecurity and Common Criteria test labs and product-certification firms (10-500 staff), including newly designated ones.
problem: Third-party conformity assessment is required for higher-risk classes under several regimes: CRA important-Class II and critical products, the radio-equipment cyber delegated act, new Machinery Regulation duties from 20 Jan 2027, and AI Act biometrics (dates from background knowledge, verify). Assessor capacity is the bottleneck. Each file review takes weeks of expert time on incomplete, inconsistent submissions, and delay lands on the manufacturer's launch date.
solution: An intake portal that bounces incomplete submissions against a clause map, an LLM-assisted cross-check of claims versus test evidence versus SBOM, auto-generated clarification requests to the manufacturer, a reviewer workbench with evidence links, and traceable report drafting. EU-hosted or on-prem for confidentiality.
why_now: CRA reporting began 11 Sep 2026 and further obligations land 11 Dec 2027, while new-body designation and accreditation are slow. File volume is about to rise faster than assessor headcount.
revenue_model: $30-120k/year per lab, or per-reviewer seats at $500-1,500/month, plus implementation fees.
non_obvious_insight: In any permit regime the scarce resource is the assessor's hours, and manufacturers pay for delay. Selling to roughly 150 known assessors is easier than selling to 100,000 manufacturers, and it produces unique data on what a 'good file' looks like.
first_30_days: Email 40 labs and notified bodies and offer to pilot on a backlog of anonymized historical files. Run three paid pilots at EUR 5-10k, measure review-hours saved, and turn the results into a case study.

title: Under-Canopy Grave Detection Survey Service
one_liner: Find unmarked graves before the bulldozer does, using drone LiDAR that sees through trees, machine-learning triage and targeted ground-penetrating radar.
customer: Municipalities, state DOTs, developers, title companies, utilities and solar or pipeline builders, plus churches and heritage nonprofits.
problem: Lost and unrecorded burial grounds are usually discovered when earthmovers hit them, causing delay, cost and heartbreak. Historic cemeteries, especially those of marginalized communities, are often undocumented. GPR surveys are slow, costly per acre and limited by scarce operators. There is no burial-risk layer in due diligence.
solution: Drone LiDAR and photogrammetry across large tracts to detect depressions and anomalies under canopy, ML-ranked into a probability map, followed by targeted GPR verification of the top candidates. Deliver a survey report and a registry entry. Add LLM reading of handwritten cemetery and church records.
why_now: Survey-grade drone LiDAR is now cheap, ML for GPR and terrain anomalies has matured, and rural land is being cleared quickly for solar, data centers and pipelines. LLMs can now read handwritten historic records. Everstory's drone mapping of about 400 cemeteries shows the method works for known sites.
revenue_model: $200-$1,500 per acre depending on terrain and depth, annual subscriptions for DOTs and utilities, and data licensing to title insurers.
non_obvious_insight: Every earthmoving project carries burial-risk liability that appears in no database. The same survey serves developers, heritage groups and families, so it can be financed by the party with the most to lose.
first_30_days: Pilot with 2 churches or heritage groups on grant-funded work. Rent a LiDAR drone and pitch 5 solar developers on due-diligence add-ons. Recruit a GPR contractor and a cultural-resources archaeologist for sign-off.

title: Protein Allocation Co-op for Mid-Size Brands
one_liner: A buyers' co-op that pools forward volume for whey and reformulates around shortages for brands too small to get allocation.
customer: Mid-size sports-nutrition, RTD beverage and bar brands (roughly $20-200M revenue) that lack direct cheese-plant relationships.
problem: Whey isolate is around $14/lb, some suppliers are sold out through 2026, and big buyers lock allocations, so small brands pay spot prices or get nothing.
solution: Aggregate members' forward demand into direct contracts with mid-size cheese and whey processors, and run a reformulation desk that blends whey with alternative proteins to spec.
why_now: The constraint is downstream whey-processing capacity and cheese output rather than raw milk, and factories are retooling for cottage cheese, so relationships and volume commitments now decide who gets protein.
revenue_model: Annual membership plus a 2-4% margin on pooled volume and fees for the reformulation desk.
non_obvious_insight: The shortage is partly a market-structure problem for small buyers rather than an absolute supply problem. Aggregation turns a set of unattractive small accounts into one large, plannable contract.
first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 brands into a founding cohort with combined tonnage, then hold calls with five mid-size cheese and whey plants to test whether they will commit capacity to a pooled buyer.

title: O-1 Evidence Vault as a Startup Employee Benefit
one_liner: Continuously captures, verifies and time-stamps the evidence that O-1A, EB-1A and NIW petitions are actually won on, so a lawyer can file in weeks instead of scrambling for six months.
customer: Venture-backed startups and AI labs with foreign-born staff pay $25-40 per employee per month. Founders, PhD students and researchers can use a self-serve tier. Immigration firms license a white-label version.
problem: The $100k fee on new H-1B petitions for workers abroad, and a wage-weighted lottery for everyone else, have pushed tech employers toward O-1A, EB-1A and NIW as the primary route. But these are evidence-driven cases. Clients show up with nothing organized, the lawyer spends weeks chasing citation counts, salary comparisons, press links and reference letters, letters end up as boilerplate, and half the evidence (paid associations, vanity press, generic membership) gets discounted by adjudicators at the final-merits stage anyway. AI-generated petitions are now a recognizable genre officers discount.
solution: A vault that connects to sources people already have (OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar, GitHub/Hugging Face adoption, patents, OpenReview and conference reviewer rosters, Wayback-archived press, compensation data with consent) and adds structured quarterly manager memos documenting the employee's critical role. It logs each independent-expert letter request with dates and independence facts. Output is a criterion-by-criterion evidence map with gaps and a plain-language six-month plan, plus a flag for evidence types officers typically discount. It hands the packet to any immigration lawyer, including the employer's existing counsel.
why_now: The H-1B fee and lottery weighting since late 2025 have made O-1A and EB-1A a mainstream path rather than an exception for founders and stars. AI labs and startups need it for dozens of employees at once, so time-to-file matters. Public scholarly and code metadata are now available through open APIs, and LLMs make it feasible to structure messy evidence at low cost.
revenue_model: Per-employee SaaS ($25-40 per month), a $300-500 one-time evidence audit, and a licensing fee from law firms. Immigration counsel remains separate, and no fee-splitting occurs.
non_obvious_insight: Petitions are decided on what was already documented by the time the client met the lawyer. Nobody builds evidence continuously because no one owns the job: HR doesn't know the criteria, lawyers only engage after the decision to file, and employees don't know what counts. Separately, the evidence that counts (independent judging, real citations, critical-role documentation) is often free to collect early and impossible to fabricate later, while the paid pay-to-play tactics sold to nervous applicants are actively harmful.
first_30_days: Find 3 seed or Series A AI startups with heavily foreign-born teams, through their immigration counsel or investor platform teams. Run a manual concierge audit for 20 employees at $300 each, producing the criterion-by-criterion map in a spreadsheet plus Google Doc. Identify the top 5 recurring evidence gaps (they will be the same across companies) and automate those first. Convert the startups to a subscription once the first two employees file petitions faster than expected.

title: Solar Defection Radar for African Utilities
one_liner: Africa's invisible solar and battery boom leaves utilities, banks and insurers blind, so measure it district by district.
customer: African distribution utilities and regulators, development finance institutions, commercial banks and insurers.
problem: Africa installs 17 GW in 2026 (+45%), 75% of it distributed. Ember's estimates are 2x official figures, and only 14 of 54 countries reported 2025 data. Utilities cannot see which paying customers are leaving, and lenders cannot price the assets.
solution: Estimate installed solar and battery stock per district from customs and import data, rooftop detection in satellite imagery and installer sales data. The wedge is a quarterly district-level report for Nigeria or Kenya, sold to one utility and one DFI.
why_now: Chinese exports hit records and batteries now outsell panels in import dollars. Ember's 'invisible boom' finding is public but nobody has productised it.
revenue_model: $25-100k per year per institution, plus bespoke studies for DFIs.
non_obvious_insight: When self-generation outruns official statistics, the first credible dataset becomes the reference for tariffs, credit and insurance pricing.
first_30_days: Combine public Chinese export data, Ember figures and roof imagery for Lagos and Kano. Give a free sample to three utilities and one DFI.

title: Narrow Networks and Reference Pricing for Pet Insurers
one_liner: Pet insurers reimburse whatever clinics invoice while losing about 10 points a year to price/mix inflation; build the pet-insurance 'PPO' from affordable-care clinics whose invoices run about 44% lower.
customer: Mid-size pet insurers and MGAs (payers), affordable-care and team-based independent clinics (network), and insured owners steered by a lower deductible or higher reimbursement in-network.
problem: 2025 premiums grew about 19.7% against 9% growth in insured animals, and insurers do not contract with clinics, so they have no lever on price. Owners face renewal shock. Corporate chains (Mars about 2,100 clinics; GoodVets going from 75 to 116) are bound to margin targets and are unlikely to cut price.
solution: Contract a metro-by-metro network of independent affordable-care clinics with agreed fee schedules, standardized service coding and direct pay. The insurer offers an in-network tier (for example, 90% reimbursement with no deductible on routine lines). We provide claims routing, spectrum-of-care quality guardrails, and network-savings reporting. Start with one metro.
why_now: The premium/enrollment gap is now visible in trade press, roll-ups are accelerating, and the affordable-care model is documented at $130 vs $233 average invoices. Model-law adoption is pushing insurers toward transparency and cost containment.
revenue_model: Shared savings (20-30% of verified savings vs a market baseline) or 3-5% administration fee on network claims. Clinics pay nothing.
non_obvious_insight: 'Reimburse at any vet' is sold as a feature, but in human health the equivalent indemnity design gave way to networks once cost trend outran wages. Steering is the only demand-side lever pet insurance has not pulled, and the low-priced independent tier is spare capacity waiting for volume.
first_30_days: Identify 15-20 team-based or low-cost independents in one metro. Get an NDA with one small insurer or MGA and pull 200 claims. Reprice them against the network fee schedule to show projected savings (target 15% or more). Propose a 6-month shared-savings pilot on an existing product tier.

title: Responsible-Charge Network for AI-Made Professional Work
one_liner: Licensed engineers and architects take legal responsibility for AI-generated permit sets per review, with a review-telemetry audit trail that also lowers malpractice premiums.
customer: AI-native firms that generate permit drawings, structural letters and MEP plans for ADUs, solar, decks and prefab, and the small design firms that use them. They need licensed sign-off in many states and don't want to employ engineers everywhere.
problem: AI can draft a permit set in an hour, but only a licensed human can seal it. Startups hire engineers state by state or rely on stamp mills. Regulators and insurers fear rubber-stamping, and 'responsible charge' (the legal standard that the professional actually directed the work) is unprovable. Existing AI-drawing companies such as Spacial keep licensed engineers in-house, so smaller entrants have no good option.
solution: A vetted network of licensed professionals paid a fixed fee per stamped package, plus software that records how the review happened: time on sheet, checks completed, redlines, overrides. That log becomes the defensible 'responsible-charge' record for state boards, and it underwrites cheaper E&O coverage through an MGA partner. Start narrow with structural and engineering letters for residential ADU, deck and solar permits in three states.
why_now: AI permit-set generators are moving from demos to real volume, and the standard practice is a licensed engineer reviewing before sealing. Professional liability carriers now ask about AI use, and licensing boards are issuing AI guidance. Nobody has built the shared review-evidence layer.
revenue_model: 25% to 35% take on engineer fees of $150 to $600 per package. MGA commission on E&O premiums. SaaS fee for the telemetry and audit-trail software.
non_obvious_insight: In AI-delivered professional services, the scarce input is not intelligence but a person who can lose a license. Whoever holds verifiable proof of actual review owns the pricing of liability, which is worth more than the stamps. The product is explicitly anti-stamp-mill: it makes shallow review visible and expensive.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 semi-retired PEs across three states. Sign two AI-permit startups or ADU designers with a backlog. Run the review flow manually with screen recordings and checklists to gather telemetry. Meet one small-firm E&O broker about a pilot rider for reviewed AI work.

title: Pallet Co-Op for Micro-Resellers
one_liner: A distributor for one-person resellers that buys store-closing truckloads, values them SKU by SKU, and splits them into size-matched $150 to $500 shares delivered to each member.
customer: Under-25 and hobbyist resellers (roughly 3 to 100 sales per week) who currently buy at retail or from other resellers. They pay a markup of 8% to 15% plus a $19 per month membership.
problem: Real wholesale margins are locked behind minimum order quantities and size-run mismatch. A liquidator lot has 240 pairs, but 60% are size 6 or size 13 that nobody wants to hold. Mystery pallets are priced as a percentage of MSRP, not by what a SKU actually resells for, so buyers overpay for junk and underbid the winners. Discord 'group buys' exist but run on trust and screenshots, and they collapse when someone ghosts on payment.
solution: We buy truckload and pallet lots from liquidators and closing retailers, run the manifest against resale comps to price every line, and slice it: each member gets a share of the SKUs and sizes they selected, with the top-value pairs allocated by lottery so nobody feels cheated. Deposits are collected before we buy, so we carry almost no inventory risk. A partnered 3PL or a garage-and-labels crew ships each member's slice within a week. Later: net-14 financing on shares and buy-back of unsold slow-moving sizes.
why_now: Retail contraction is producing a steady stream of liquidation lots in 2025-26: Foot Locker is being folded into Dick's with store consolidation, other mall and footwear chains are closing doors, and brands reset inventory after tariff and demand swings. Margins on hyped Nike pairs are thin, so only good buying keeps micro-resellers alive. Cheap vision models make manifest-to-comp valuation nearly free.
revenue_model: 8% to 15% markup on each share plus $19 per month membership. Later, interest on short-term inventory financing and fees for a 'sell-through insurance' tier.
non_obvious_insight: Capital is not what stops small resellers from wholesale. Break-bulk is. Nobody sells a truckload in 40 slices sorted by size. The person who does the boring sorting, allocating and shipping becomes the small reseller's Costco. Because valuation uses resale comps rather than MSRP percent, the co-op can quietly outbid mystery-pallet buyers on the best lots.
first_30_days: Find one liquidator willing to sell a 5 to 10 pallet lot of mixed sneakers and apparel. Pre-sell 40 slots at $250 each in a Discord with deposits before buying anything, using the manifest value as the pitch. Rent a garage or use a local prep center. Ship in 10 days, collect testimonials and reviews, then run the next lot every week.

title: CRA Continuity Kit for One-Person Vendors
one_liner: An outsourced EU Cyber Resilience Act desk that handles the 24h/72h/14-day vulnerability reporting clock and keeps a signed 10-year release vault with a dead-man's-switch escrow, built for micro-vendors with no security team.
customer: Solo and micro hardware, firmware, app and SaaS vendors that sell into the EU, such as ESP32 and Raspberry Pi based device makers on Tindie or Crowd Supply, small GmbHs, and indie app publishers. There is no size exemption. They pay EUR 79-399/month per product.
problem: CRA Article 14 reporting began 11 September 2026: a 24-hour early warning, a 72-hour notification and a 14-day final report via ENISA's Single Reporting Platform, with fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. A one-person German GmbH selling firmware asks how to comply given CE marking, a technical file, 'every security update you ship has to stay available for 10 years' and no size threshold. Maintainers are already bailing out: the croniter fork was archived citing the CRA.
solution: A subscription that provides (1) a named on-call reporting desk that prepares and files the early warning, notification and final report on the vendor's delegated authority against a pre-agreed playbook; (2) SBOM generation and continuous vulnerability watch tied to the customer's release artifacts, to detect an 'actively exploited' trigger; (3) an immutable, signed release vault holding every shipped update for 10+ years, with a dead-man's-switch: if the vendor stops responding or dissolves, the firmware source and update artifacts are released to customers or a nominated steward; (4) a fixed-price 'CRA readiness sprint' that produces the technical-file skeleton and declaration-of-conformity scaffolding.
why_now: The reporting obligation went live 11 September 2026, so this is a forced-spend deadline, not a forecast. Full obligations follow in December 2027. Legal commentators say many still associate the CRA only with consumer IoT and are unprepared.
revenue_model: EUR 1,500 fixed-price readiness sprint, then EUR 79-399/month per product for the reporting retainer and vault, tiered by product count and risk class. Optional per-incident filing fee. Channel deals with device marketplaces and Linux/embedded distributors.
non_obvious_insight: The gap is not compliance dashboards (the Ask HN thread already lists Vulert, ReARM and the ORC WG hub) but staffed responsiveness and durable custody: a solo founder cannot staff a 24-hour clock or credibly promise 10 years of availability. A dead-man's-switch vault turns the founder's bus-factor into a compliance asset. Escrow at end of life is a recurring HN demand, e.g. 'When you release a product, you should be required to put the source code in escrow, so it can be released at EoL' https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44531176, and vendors ask for escrow tooling https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46402528. Evidence of demand: one-person GmbH asking for help https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49520688; obligations and fines https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/09/11/eus-cyber-resilience-act-starts-the-24-hour-vulnerability-clock/5295821; croniter archived https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43168860.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 design partners from the Open Regulatory Compliance WG CRA hub, Torizon CRA summit attendees, and Tindie/Crowd Supply sellers, plus the author of the Ask HN thread. Sell the EUR 1,500 sprint with a written 24h playbook and SBOM pipeline for their repos. Stand up the vault on object-lock storage with signed manifests and a heartbeat check-in. Have a CRA-literate lawyer review the delegation-of-filing template. Convert sprint customers to the retainer.
